newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Penniless Russian institute is radioactive threat.
newsitem.headline: Penniless Russian institute is radioactive threat.

text.p: A Russian scientist said on Monday a Chernobyl-style disaster could happen just outside Moscow because his institute could not afford to dispose of its large quantities of highly radioactive material.

"At present the conditions of radioactivity at the institute are more or less normal but nobody can predict the moment when a serious accident may happen," said Sergei Mund, director of the Elektrogorsk Institute for Oil Processing.
Located on the institute's premises are 663 rods of cobalt-60, a highly radioactive material used in a wide range of scientific research from space satellites to medicine.
"Eighty percent of the rods need to be decommissioned now but it is a complex and costly operation and we just don't have the money," Mund told Reuters in an interview.
The pen-sized rods, encased in steel, are stored in water tanks where their high electron activity gives them a blue glow. Scientists regularly check the water's radioactivity levels.
"In the worst case scenario, if the power or water supply failed, we could face an explosion, a fire and the subsequent contamination of a 100 square kilometre area," said Mund.
Elektrogorsk, a small town of about 20,000, lies just 70 km (45 miles) east of Moscow.
"If there were an accident and the wind was blowing from the east we could have quite a problem on our hands," said Mund.
Up to 300,000 people would be directly affected and the whole region would suffer abnormally high levels of radioactivity for many years to come.
The institute is, in many ways, a microcosm of the problems plaguing Russian science in the post-communist era.

Its scientists -- down to just 10 from 40 a couple of years ago -- have not been paid since September. Most are elderly and have nowhere else to go. The average monthly salary is 300,000 roubles ($54).
With no funds for any meaningful research, they are engaged full time in trying to monitor radioactivity levels and ensuring that the unthinkable does not happen.
Decommissioning the radioactive rods would cost at least six billion roubles ($1.1 million), well beyond the means of either the institute or the local government, Mund said.
"Nobody denies we have a problem but the matter gets passed from one commission to the next and no money ever arrives," said Anatoly Platov, one of the institute's scientists.
He said one worry was erosion of the metal cases containing the cobalt. Holes in the casing would allow radioactivity to escape into the water and into the atmosphere.
"I am a pensioner already but we have to keep working here trying to keep the situation under control. After all, we live here, we are the front line," Platov added.
Russia's cash-strapped government has acknowledged the problem of radioactive waste.

Environment minister Viktor Danilov-Danilyan recently told Reuters in an interview that disposing of radioactive waste would cost Russia $700 billion. The country's 1996 gross domestic product (GDP) only came to about $400 billion.
Mund said the growing shortage of properly qualified staff was impairing the institute's ability to maintain adequate safety standards.
Ironically, the institute has in the past conducted research into the consequences of the world's worst nuclear disaster at Chernobyl, which sent radioactive clouds across Europe in 1986.

One former nuclear physicist who worked at Chernobyl after the accident said he thought Elektrogorsk posed a serious risk but added that there were many other sites in and around Moscow that were equally or even more dangerous.
"There are 16 nuclear reactors in Moscow alone," said Nikolai Vasilyev, who has now found more lucrative work as a chauffeur.
"Elektrogorsk is being kept running by a group of pensioners but you need a lot of people to maintain such a plant.
"Many people were working to keep Chernobyl safe but this did not prevent a disaster," he added.
